claims.text: The ab initio Z method is less computationally demanding than full thermodynamic integration.
The ab initio Z method is suitable for high-throughput calculation of melting properties of refractory materials.
In the Z method, microcanonical ab initio molecular dynamics is used to heat a material until spontaneous melting occurs.
The solid is metastable near its superheating limit before the spontaneous melting event.
Sufficiently large simulation supercells minimize finite-size effects.
An interface forms between solid and emerging liquid regions during the transition.
The solid remains metastable during heating until a critical energy is reached.
Reaching the critical energy causes a spontaneous solid-to-liquid phase transition.
The spontaneous melting transition is characterized by a sudden drop in temperature.
The melting temperature can be deduced from the spontaneous transition observed in a Z-method trajectory.
Fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change can be deduced from the spontaneous transition.
The Z method will yield a melting temperature close to that obtained using full free-energy integration.
The Z method will yield fusion enthalpy, entropy, and volume-change estimates consistent with full free-energy integration.
Z-method results will be reproducible across multiple simulation runs when finite-size effects are controlled.
Traditional ab initio free-energy methods based on thermodynamic integration are more accurate than the Z method.
Traditional ab initio thermodynamic integration is computationally expensive and unsuitable for high-throughput studies.
Strong anharmonic effects may limit the accuracy of the Z method.
A simulation supercell that is too small may limit the accuracy of the Z method.
The Z method has shown promise for estimating melting properties.
